passages.t: A curse on the day of his birth
passages.happening:
‘After this, Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth’ (verse 1).

“May the day of my birth perish” (verse 3), he says, and the night he was conceived. “If only that day had turned to darkness! May God above disregard it; may no light shine upon it” (verse 4). He asks darkness, gloom and cloud to swallow it, and the night to be struck from the calendar, barren, with no joyful voice in it. Let it be cursed by those who curse days, by those ready to rouse Leviathan. Let its morning stars go dark and its dawn never come.

Why? “For that night did not shut the doors of the womb to hide the sorrow from my eyes” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
After seven days of silence Job speaks, and the book changes from prose to poetry. The patient Job of chapters 1 and 2 now pours out a lament of astonishing bitterness. He does not curse God, as the accuser predicted. He curses his own existence.

In the ancient world curses were serious acts, but Job does not expect this one to work. The day is long past. It is a poet's way of wishing his life undone. And it runs creation backward. Where God said let there be light (Genesis 1:3), Job says let that day be darkness.

Leviathan was a sea monster that stands in several biblical texts as a figure of chaos (Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1). Job may be alluding to sorcerers thought able to curse days and stir up chaos. The line is difficult. Some scholars change one vowel to read those who curse the sea instead of the day, which pairs naturally with Leviathan, and translations differ. The creature will return at the end of the book, under God's hand (chapter 41).

The word for deep darkness in verse 5, tsalmavet, is the word of Psalm 23:4, the shadow of death.
passages.later: The prophet Jeremiah, in his own anguish, said almost the same: “Cursed be the day I was born! May the day my mother bore me never be blessed” (Jeremiah 20:14).
passages.asks: Job did not hide his anguish, and the Bible did not hide it either. Ask whether you have words for your own darkest days, or whether you have only kept them in. And ask who could hear them from you.

passages.t: Why he wishes he had died at birth
passages.happening:
Now the curse turns to a question: “Why did I not perish at birth; why did I not die as I came from the womb?” (verse 11). Why were there knees to receive him and breasts to nurse him?

If he had died, he says, he would be at rest, “with kings and counselors of the earth, who built for themselves cities now in ruins” (verse 14), and with princes who filled their houses with silver.

He pictures the grave as a place of quiet. “There the wicked cease from raging, and there the weary find rest” (verse 17). Prisoners are at ease there and do not hear the voice of the slave driver. “Both small and great are there, and the slave is freed from his master” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The word why marks the turn from curse to lament.

Knees to receive a child may reflect the custom of placing a newborn on a father's knees to acknowledge it as his own (Genesis 50:23).

The grave Job pictures is Sheol, the common Old Testament picture of the place of the dead, where all go regardless of rank. The ancient world was full of the ruins of cities and palaces built by kings long dead, and the image would have been familiar to any reader who had seen their mounds.

This is not a full teaching about life after death. It is a lament. Job imagines death as quiet rest because life has become unbearable. His words about a stillborn child in verse 16 are about his own wish not to have lived. They say nothing about any child who died, or about the parents who grieve them.
passages.later: Jeremiah asked the same question: “Why did I come out of the womb to see only trouble and sorrow, and to end my days in shame?” (Jeremiah 20:18).
passages.asks: Job longed for rest, and he could not imagine finding it anywhere but the grave. Ask where you look for rest when you are worn out. And ask who around you is weary in a way you have not noticed.

passages.t: Why is light given to the miserable?
passages.happening:
Job widens the question to all who suffer: “Why is light given to the miserable, and life to the bitter of soul, who long for death that does not come, and search for it like hidden treasure” (verses 20-21).

“Why is life given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?” (verse 23). He sighs when food is put before him, and his groans pour out like water.

“For the thing I feared has overtaken me, and what I dreaded has befallen me. I am not at ease or quiet; I have no rest, for trouble has come” (verses 25-26).
passages.hearers:
Job's question now belongs to everyone in pain, not only to him.

Notice the word hedged in, verse 23. The accuser used a closely related word in 1:10 for the protecting hedge God had placed around Job. What was once protection now feels to Job like a prison. He does not know what the reader knows.

The last verse is breathless, a list of what he lacks: ease, quiet, rest. The poem ends without an answer, and the book does not rush to give one. Eliphaz will speak next, and everything the friends say for many chapters is a reply to the anguish first spoken here.
passages.later: Elijah, worn out and afraid, prayed the same prayer under a broom tree: “Take my life, for I am no better than my fathers” (1 Kings 19:4). God's answer to him was sleep, food and water, and a quiet voice.
passages.hard:
Job longs for death. Is it wrong to wish you had never been born?

Some readers think Job's lament crosses a line into despair and ingratitude. Others note that Job does not curse God, that the Bible records the same kind of words from Jeremiah (Jeremiah 20:14-18), and that the Psalms hold laments as dark as this one, Psalm 88 among them. Above all, the LORD says at the end that Job has spoken rightly of him (42:7). Most interpreters conclude that these are the words of a man in agony, and that the book includes them to show that faith can bring its darkest feelings into the open, before God.

The book does not scold Job for these words, and it does not leave him in them either. His lament is the beginning of a long struggle that brings him at last to meet God. The words are given so that pain can be spoken. They are not the last word, and the longing for death is not where Job's story ends.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Job asked why, and he asked it out loud. Ask whether you believe God can bear your questions. And if your own darkness is heavy right now, ask who you could tell today.
